concept.name: Payment versus payment
concept.definition: A foreign exchange settlement mechanism that ensures the final transfer of one currency occurs if and only if the final transfer of the countercurrency occurs, eliminating FX settlement (Herstatt) risk — the loss of the full value of a currency paid without receiving the currency bought.
concept.intuition: Both currency legs of an FX trade move simultaneously; you can never wire your dollars away and get no euros back because the other bank failed that afternoon.
concept.mechanics: A PvP system (notably CLS Bank, per BIS analysis of FX settlement risk) holds both sides' payment instructions and releases the two currency transfers together; where PvP is unavailable, legs settle in different payment systems and time zones, exposing the paying party until the counterleg arrives.
concept.failure_modes: PvP eliminates principal risk but not liquidity risk (a party may fail to fund its side, unwinding the day's queue) or replacement-cost risk (re-doing the trade at a worse rate); coverage gaps leave non-eligible currencies and counterparties exposed.
concept.misconceptions: PvP is not automatic in FX — it requires settlement through a PvP mechanism such as CLS, and a large share of global FX turnover historically settled with one leg at risk (the 1974 Bankhaus Herstatt failure being the canonical loss).
concept.example: A USD/EUR trade settles through CLS: the member's dollar payment and euro receipt are released simultaneously at settlement, so neither bank is exposed for the full principal if the other fails intraday.

citations.source: BIS CPMI, Glossary of payments and market infrastructure terminology
BIS, Settlement risk in foreign exchange transactions (CPSS, March 1996)
